input: In this example, consideration is given to a continuous stirred-tank reactor in which a neutralisation reaction is carried out, the reaction being first order with respect to the limiting reactant. The rate constant at the operating temperature has a value of 0.041 min-1, and the mean residence time within the vessel is 23 min. When the standard ideal-CSTR design relation is applied at steady state, the conversion of the limiting reactant is obtained as 48.5%. The result follows from a steady-state material balance written over the limiting reactant: under steady conditions, the amount of reactant entering with the feed must be accounted for by the amount leaving with the product stream together with the amount consumed by reaction throughout the vessel volume. Since the ideal vessel is assumed to be perfectly mixed, the concentration at every point in the vessel is identical to the outlet concentration, so the reaction rate throughout the volume is governed by that single concentration. It follows that the conversion is determined by the balance between the rate constant and the residence time, increasing steadily as the residence time is extended and approaching complete conversion in the limit; at a residence time of 23 min, the stated rate constant leads to the conversion quoted above. By way of comparison, a plug-flow vessel of the same volume would be expected to achieve a somewhat higher conversion, because the concentration declines progressively along the flow path. It should be noted that the estimate rests on two underlying assumptions, namely perfect mixing and constant density, the latter ensuring that the residence time can be treated as a fixed ratio of volume to volumetric flow rate. No tracer tests have yet been carried out on the actual vessel, so its residence-time distribution remains uncharacterised; phenomena such as dead volume or bypassing, if they occur, would tend to depress the conversion actually achieved below 48.5%.
target: A continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.041 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time is 23 min. The steady-state conversion of the limiting reactant is 48.5% for an ideal CSTR. The conversion comes from the steady-state balance on the limiting reactant. At steady state, the reactant that enters with the feed is balanced by the reactant that leaves with the product and the reactant consumed by reaction in the vessel volume. Because an ideal CSTR is perfectly mixed, the concentration everywhere in the vessel is the outlet concentration, and the reaction rate in the whole volume is set by that concentration. The conversion therefore depends on the product of the rate constant and the residence time measured against that product plus one: as the residence time grows, the conversion rises towards complete conversion, and at 23 min the stated rate gives the stated figure. A plug-flow vessel of equal volume would give a higher conversion for the same feed, because its concentration falls along the flow path and the rate is higher over most of the volume. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density. Constant density makes the residence time a fixed ratio of vessel volume to volumetric flow, and perfect mixing is the assumption that sets the rate. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run. The residence-time distribution of the actual vessel is therefore unmeasured: dead volume would shorten the effective residence time, and bypassing would pass part of the feed through almost unreacted. Either fault would bring the actual conversion below 48.5%. The figure is the conversion of the ideal vessel at the stated conditions, and its application to the actual vessel rests on mixing behaviour that has not been verified.
